extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and practitioners interested in philosophy of science, scientific method, and methodology of inquiry
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for choosing, conducting, and judging methods of scientific inquiry (a priori/deductive, a posteriori/observational, and experimental), especially for complex phenomena involving many concurrent causes. Emphasizes when each method is applicable, necessary precautions for experiments, and the requirement of verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express causal laws as tendencies, not absolute results
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws of causation, because they can be counteracted, should be stated in words affirmative of tendencies only, and not of actual results (e.g., bodies 'tend' to move, forces exert 'pressure').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation and examples: the body 'tends' to continue motion even when counteracted; say 'tendency' rather than asserting actual motion. Use terminology (like 'pressure' in mechanics) that signifies tendency. Avoid phrasing laws as categorical true/false statements that invite the notion of exceptions; the correct view is that laws state tendencies which may be modified by concurrent causes (balloon vs. falling bodies; sun and moon example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat concurrent principles as a law and its exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Where two causes concurrently influence an effect, it is incorrect to call one the law and the other an exception; both are comprehensive rules acting together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance and example: The so-called 'exception' (e.g., atmospheric resistance preventing a balloon from falling) is itself a real concurrent principle which acts in all cases (it retards all falls). Classify concurrent effects under concurrent principles rather than 'rule' versus 'exception.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose method type appropriately (a priori deduction vs. a posteriori observation/experiment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three general modes of inquiry: deductive (a priori) inference from laws of separate causes, and a posteriori methods which split into pure observation (collating instances) and experiment (operating upon causes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the a priori method when direct observation/experiment are infeasible for complex phenomena; use experiment when you can operate on causes in sufficiently ascertained circumstances; pure observation (method of agreement) is often inapplicable for effects arising from many causes (mercury example). Clarify which method you mean to use and why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of pure observation (Method of Agreement / plurality of causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple collation of instances (observational method) is generally inapplicable to phenomena that result from many concurrent causes, because the same effect can occur without a particular agent, and that agent can fail to produce effect without other concurring influences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and implications: Recovery from disease may occur with or without a drug because many other influences exist. Even large collections of observational returns may only show weak associations ('rather more recoveries') and be of secondary value. Do not rely on mere agreement of instances when plurality_of_causes exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental method requires well-ascertained and controlled circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: When devising experiments, introduce the agent into circumstances which are exactly ascertained, and exclude or make computable any other causes whose effects might be confounded with the agent’s effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical precautions: ascertain the pre-existing circumstances of each case (age, sex, disease stage, etc.), exclude confounders or be able to compute and subtract their influence, multiply experiments in varied circumstances to reduce chance of unknown causes being present in all. The difficulty of meeting these conditions is acute in physiology and social science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical/experimental inquiry must avoid surreptitious deduction to be genuinely empirical
rubrics_metrics.description: If the 'experimental' method uses prior knowledge of the simpler modus operandi of components to reason about the complex case, then it is in fact a deductive procedure, not a purely empirical one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish pure experimentation (operating directly on the complex case without appealing to prior deductions about component tendencies) from experiments that are effectively deductive because they rely on previously known laws. When claiming an empirical test, ensure it isn't covertly deductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference is unreliable when other causes act during the transition or when comparable cases cannot be found
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparing the same case before and after an intervention, or comparing two different cases, fails to isolate the effect if other causes operate in the intervening period or if truly identical cases differing in only one respect are unobtainable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume pre/post comparisons or cross-case comparisons establish causation in complex settings where other influences change during transition or exact matching of cases is impossible. The Method of Difference is 'entirely unavailing' for intermixtures of effects in many real-world phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Concomitant Variations is useful but encumbered in complex phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Using covariation between cause and effect can sometimes help ascertain a cause’s law, but it is limited and 'not less encumbered' than more elementary methods in complicated subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply concomitant variations cautiously; it can assist in discerning tendencies where separation of causes is impracticable, but it will often be inadequate in highly interwoven systems (physiology, social science). Use it as a supplementary tool, not a panacea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only sufficiently potent causes yield clear experimental truths amid many concurrent causes
rubrics_metrics.description: When an agent's tendency is small relative to competing influences, its effect will often be hidden; only agents that succeed in a large proportion of cases against opposing causes can be established experimentally (examples: quinine, colchicum, lime-juice, cod-liver oil).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate effect size and consistency: large, robust tendencies can be experimentally established even in messy contexts; small tendencies require more controlled conditions or different methods. Expect many candidate causes to be masked by other influences unless they are notably potent.

rubrics_metrics.name: For social and political phenomena, observational and experimental methods are especially inapplicable due to extreme plurality of causes
rubrics_metrics.description: In politics and history, causes are innumerable and constantly changing, making collation of instances and artificial experiments (even if feasible) largely incapable of yielding reliable inductive conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware simplistic Baconian inductions about institutions or policies (e.g., 'a country prospered under X so X is good'); changes in many concurrent causes and temporal shifts vitiate such reasoning. Use deductive methods grounded in known laws of human action where appropriate, and be extremely cautious about causal claims from mere historical collation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive method prerequisite: ascertain laws of each separate cause (by induction or prior deduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Deductive Method’s first requisite is knowledge of the laws of the separate tendencies that combine to produce the complex effect; these premises must themselves have an inductive or experimentally-derived basis (or be deduced from simpler laws ultimately grounded in induction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before attempting ratiocination from causes to effect, obtain (by experiment, observation, or prior deduction grounded in induction) reliable laws for each contributing cause. In many domains (physiology, social science) this step is the major difficulty and determines whether deduction will succeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study tendencies in cases where they operate alone or with calculable agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: To discover the law of a tendency, study it in instances where it operates alone, or only with agencies whose effects can be calculated and allowed for; laws should not be inferred from only counteracted or heavily compounded instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose experimental or observational instances where the tendency is not mixed with unknown interfering causes. When separation is impossible, use methods (pathology, carefully selected cases) that approximate isolation, or rely on deduction from simpler causes whose laws are better known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification is essential: deductions must be compared with observation and anomalies explained
rubrics_metrics.description: The third component of Deductive Method (Verification) requires that deductive conclusions be carefully compared with direct observation wherever possible; confirmed agreement permits reliance elsewhere; discrepancies demand showing what frustrated the deduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verification is the test that shields deduction from the objections about omitted or misestimated causes. If deductions fail to match experience, provide probable accounts of what prevented the expected effect. Without verification, deductive results are little more than conjecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratiocination (calculation) step: deduce effects from laws of causes but expect practical mathematical limits
rubrics_metrics.description: After ascertaining laws of causes, the second stage is to compute or reason what effect a given combination will produce; this may require advanced mathematics and is often intractable (examples: three-body problem, projectile motion with air, wind, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that even with accurate component laws, combining them into a precise prediction can exceed available mathematical methods or be practically infeasible; accept approximate reasoning where exact calculation is impossible and justify approximations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pathological facts and artificial interventions in physiology when true separation is impracticable
rubrics_metrics.description: Pathological disturbances and deliberate experimental interventions (e.g., nerve section, administering an agent) can serve as valuable equivalents to controlled experiments, by producing relatively localized disturbances that reveal causal relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer observing early stages of pathology to infer local causes before systemic reactions develop. Artificial experiments in otherwise healthy states are often better for uncovering general laws. But be mindful that constitutional or systemic disturbances obscure causal direction and that prolonged disturbances involve many secondary effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer experimental cases where circumstances can be most accurately ascertained (health over disease for general laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: When designing experiments intended to discover general laws (not just practical answers), select cases whose circumstances can be best ascertained—typically experiments on health rather than disease—because the latter are changeable and harder to predict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For investigations aiming at general laws, choose conditions that are stable and whose background influences are known; disease states are prone to unknown agencies and sequential effects that complicate inference. If using disease cases, focus on early, localized derangements with known chronology.
